hints: Model the matrix as a directed graph using only orthogonally adjacent cells with a strict value increase.
Because values must strictly increase along every edge, the directed graph cannot contain a cycle.
A topological-layer process can compute the longest path length without exploring every possible path.
Start from cells that have no larger orthogonal neighbor and process downward one layer at a time.
title: Maximum-Length Increasing Path in a Matrix

notes: A move is valid only between orthogonally adjacent cells whose values are strictly increasing along the path.
The matrix is non-empty and rectangular under the documented constraints.
The longest path length is always between 1 and m * n inclusive.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: The longest increasing path is [3, 4, 5, 6]. Moving diagonally is not allowed.
A single cell forms an increasing path of length 1.

content.problemStatement:
With an `m x n` integers `matrix`, output *the length of the longest increasing path in* `matrix`.

From each cell, you can either move in four directions: left, right, up, or down. You **may not** move **diagonally** or move **outside the boundary** (i.e., wrap-around is not allowed).

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/01/05/grid1.jpg)

```
Input: matrix = [[9,9,4],[6,6,8],[2,1,1]]
Output: 4
Explanation: The longest increasing path is [1, 2, 6, 9].
```

**Example 2:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/01/27/tmp-grid.jpg)

```
Input: matrix = [[3,4,5],[3,2,6],[2,2,1]]
Output: 4
Explanation: The longest increasing path is [3, 4, 5, 6]. Moving diagonally is not allowed.
```

**Example 3:**

```
Input: matrix = [[1]]
Output: 1
```

**Constraints:**

* `m == matrix.length`
* `n == matrix[i].length`
* `1 <= m, n <= 200`
* `0 <= matrix[i][j] <= 2^31 - 1`

notes: All advertised boilerplates implement the same O(m * n) topological-layering solution.
The solution uses only orthogonal moves and strict value increases.
Strictly increasing moves make the directed graph acyclic even when the underlying matrix grid contains cycles.
Layer count in the reverse topological process equals the maximum number of vertices on a directed path.
solution.approach: Treat each matrix cell as a node in a directed acyclic graph, with an edge from a smaller-valued cell to a larger-valued orthogonal neighbor. Compute each cell's number of larger neighbors as its incoming-edge count for a reverse topological traversal. Start from local maxima, remove edges toward smaller neighbors level by level, and count the number of levels; that count equals the longest increasing path length.

better.complexity: O(m * n) time and O(m * n) auxiliary space, plus recursion stack up to O(m * n) in the worst case.
better.description: Use DFS with memoization. Let dp[r][c] be the longest increasing path starting at cell (r,c). Compute each state once and take the maximum over all starting cells.

optimal.complexity: O(m * n) time and O(m * n) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Use reverse topological BFS. Give each cell an indegree equal to its number of larger orthogonal neighbors. Local maxima start in the queue. Remove edges toward smaller neighbors in layers; the number of processed layers is exactly the longest increasing path length.

bruteForce.complexity: Exponential time in the worst case; O(m * n) recursion/visited state only if explicitly tracked.
bruteForce.description: Run a DFS from every cell and explore every valid increasing path without memoization. This recomputes the same suffix paths many times and can take exponential time in the number of cells.

followUps: How would the DFS + memoization solution compare with the topological-layer solution in recursion depth and implementation risk?
What changes would be required if diagonal moves were allowed?
Can the algorithm be adapted to report one actual longest increasing path in addition to its length?
What would change if equal-valued moves were allowed?
learningObjectives: Model a grid problem as a directed acyclic graph.
Recognize when strict inequalities guarantee acyclicity.
Apply memoization and topological sorting to longest-path problems in DAGs.
Analyze time and auxiliary-space complexity for matrix algorithms.
